newsitem.title: UK: Major says he can still win British election.
newsitem.headline: Major says he can still win British election.

text.p: With only five days to go until Britain's election, Prime Minister John Major insisted he could still achieve victory despite evidence of a massive swing to Labour.
As the long election campaign drew to an end, concern mounted that Irish guerrillas might try to disrupt the May 1 poll and election officials were sent instructions on how to deal with bomb threats.
In a television interview with ITN on Friday, Major brushed aside opinion polls which show him well behind the opposition Labour Party, insisting that the tide was turning in his favour.
"Things are changing...That there is a change, and there has been for some days, I think is beyond doubt," Major said. "I don't know who's ahead at the moment, I make no assertion that we're behind."
An opinion poll in Saturday's Daily Telegraph newspaper showed Labour 16 points ahead of the ruling Conservatives, unchanged from the previous day.
Major said many voters were still undecided, and appealed to disaffected Conservative supporters to vote for him rather than staying away from the polls.

"There are a lot of people still to make up their minds, and if they were going to vote for our opponents I think they would have made up their minds," he said. "My message to people is -- don't sit this election out. There's a very great deal at stake."

An increasingly rancorous tone to the campaign was evident, with the Conservatives accusing Labour leader Tony Blair of lying about Conservative pension policies to strike fear into Britain's pensioners.
Major accused Labour of "scurrilous, unscrupulous campaigning" and Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine launched a bitter attack on Blair's integrity.
"You are not fit to be leader of the Labour Party and you are certainly not fit to be Prime Minister of Britain," he said at a Conservative rally.

Heseltine said Blair had "cynically played with the fears and emotions of the elderly and frail". But Blair stood behind his assertion that the Conservatives would replace the basic state pension with a privately funded scheme.

Earlier, Britain sent guidelines to hundreds of election officials on how to respond to any attempt by Irish guerrillas to disrupt the election, as bomb attacks and security alerts again caused traffic chaos in England.
Thousands of polling venues were expected to be screened for explosives before voting starts on May 1, and searches of voters were also likely, officials said.

For the first time ever, officials running the election in each constituency were sent details of how to cope with bomb threats. The aim was to "enable the electoral process to continue uninterrupted unless that would pose a clear risk to public safety", the guidelines said.
"Should a bomb threat be received, the police will assess its credibility and consider, in the light of the security measures in place, what level of response is appropriate."
Severe disruption could even result in voting being postponed to the following day, the document said.

The Irish Republican Army, which is fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, was believed to be behind Friday's travel chaos, as part of a strategy to wring concessions from Britain's government through causing mass disruption.

Two bombs on a major motorway in central England, a suspicious device in Luton airport and a security alert in Birmingham's main railway station snarled Britain's transport system for the third time since last Friday.
